questions.stem: A 33 year old man has noticed his right testis feels heavy for 3 months. He has no pain, fever or urinary symptoms. His temperature is 36.7°C. There is a hard, craggy, non-tender mass within the right testis. It does not transilluminate and the examiner can get above it.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A painless, hard, craggy, non-transilluminating mass within the testis in a man aged 15 to 35 is testicular cancer, usually a germ cell tumour.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: hard, craggy, non-tender mass within the right testis
steps.x: Painless, hard, intratesticular and solid in a young man.

elim: Fluctuant, extra-testicular and felt separately from the testis.
Painful and tender, often with fever and dysuria.
Soft and transilluminates, with the testis inside the fluid.
A left-sided 'bag of worms' from venous dilatation, not a hard testicular mass.

steps.x: D. Testicular cancer. Painless hard testicular lump in a young man = testicular cancer until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has a 6 week history of a painless swelling of his left scrotum. He has no fever or dysuria. The swelling is confined to the scrotum and the testis cannot be felt separately from it. A pen torch is used to examine the swelling.
questions.q: Which finding would most strongly suggest a testicular tumour rather than a hydrocele?
o: The examiner can get above the swelling
The swelling is soft and fluctuant
questions.e: A tumour is a solid, hard mass that does not transilluminate; a hydrocele is a soft, fluid-filled swelling around the testis that transilluminates.

steps.x: The question asks: Which finding would most strongly suggest a testicular tumour rather than a hydrocele? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: painless swelling of his left scrotum
steps.x: Transillumination separates fluid from solid.

elim: True of both a hydrocele and a tumour.
True of both.
Both are usually painless.
Describes a fluid-filled hydrocele.

steps.x: B. The swelling does not transilluminate. Solid, non-transilluminating = tumour; transilluminating = hydrocele.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man found a painless lump in his left scrotum while showering. He has no urinary symptoms. His temperature is 36.6°C. The lump is hard and craggy. Scrotal ultrasound later confirms a testicular germ cell tumour.
questions.q: Which finding on examination would most likely have distinguished it from an epididymal cyst?
o: It could be felt separately from the testis
It could not be felt separately from the testis
It lay at the head of the epididymis
questions.e: A tumour lies within the testis and cannot be separated from it; an epididymal cyst is a benign, fluctuant, extra-testicular swelling in the head of the epididymis, felt separately.

steps.x: The question asks: Which finding on examination would most likely have distinguished it from an epididymal cyst? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
An intratesticular solid tumour.

elim: Typical of an epididymal cyst.
Typical of an epididymal cyst.
Fluid-filled cysts transilluminate.
Describes a cyst.

steps.x: B. It could not be felt separately from the testis. Tumour = within the testis; epididymal cyst = separate from it.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man had a right orchidectomy for a seminoma 5 years ago and has been well since. He now notices a painless hard nodule in the left testis. He has no family history of cancer and both testes descended normally at birth. His temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor in his history?
questions.e: Risk factors for testicular cancer include previous testicular cancer, cryptorchidism and a family history.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important risk factor in his history? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: right orchidectomy for a seminoma 5 years ago
steps.x: A previous testicular tumour.

elim: Both testes descended normally.
He has no family history.
He has not had it.
Not a risk factor.

steps.x: D. Previous testicular cancer. Previous testicular cancer raises the risk in the other testis.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man and his partner have been unable to conceive for 3 years. Semen analysis shows a low sperm count. His testes descended normally and there is no family history of cancer. He does not smoke. A routine scrotal ultrasound shows a 9 mm hypoechoic intratesticular lesion.
questions.q: Which factor in his history most increases his risk of testicular cancer?
questions.e: Infertile men are about 3 times more likely to develop testicular cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which factor in his history most increases his risk of testicular cancer? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Male subfertility.

elim: Not a risk factor.
Lowers rather than raises his risk.
Not relevant to his risk.
A test, not a risk factor.

steps.x: A. Infertility. Infertility triples the risk of testicular cancer.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has a 10 month history of a slowly enlarging painless swelling of his right testis. There is a smooth, firm, non-tender mass within the testis. Ultrasound shows a homogeneous intratesticular mass. CT shows no spread. Investigations show a normal AFP.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological type?
questions.e: Seminoma accounts for about half of testicular cancers, grows slowly, stays confined to the testis longer and never produces AFP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely histological type? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Slow growth, normal AFP, localised.

elim: Aggressive, with very high hCG and early haematogenous spread.
A non-seminoma, usually with raised AFP and faster growth.
Grows faster in younger men with raised AFP.
Produces AFP, which is normal here.

steps.x: C. Seminoma. Slow-growing, AFP normal = seminoma.

questions.stem: An 18 year old man has a 4 week history of a rapidly enlarging hard lump in his left testis. He has a dry cough. His temperature is 36.9°C. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous, partly cystic intratesticular mass. Investigations show a markedly raised AFP.
questions.q: Which is the most likely tumour type?
questions.e: Teratomas and other non-seminomatous germ cell tumours present younger, grow and metastasise faster and are associated with raised AFP and hCG.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely tumour type? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Young, fast growing, AFP raised.

elim: A sex cord-stromal tumour that does not produce AFP.
Testicular lymphoma usually affects men over 60.
Slower-growing in older men, and never produces AFP.
A rare stromal tumour without raised AFP.

steps.x: E. Teratoma. Young + rapid + AFP high = non-seminoma such as teratoma.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has had a radical orchidectomy for an embryonal carcinoma. He has a dull central back ache. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 74 bpm. Abdominal and inguinal examination are normal. Staging CT has been performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the CT scan?
questions.e: Testicular cancer spreads first to the retroperitoneal (para-aortic) nodes, which can cause back pain; endometrial and ovarian cancers also spread to these nodes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on the CT scan? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Back ache after a germ cell tumour.

elim: Not the drainage of the testis.
The scrotal skin drains here, but the testis drains to the para-aortic nodes.
Less common than nodal spread.
Not the typical pattern of spread.

steps.x: C. Enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes. Testis drains to para-aortic nodes, not inguinal.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a 3 week history of coughing up streaks of blood and a hard swelling in his right testis. His temperature is 36.9°C, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Multiple rounded masses in both lungs ('cannonball' metastases).

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the chest X-ray findings?
o: Metastases from a testicular germ cell tumour
questions.e: Testicular germ cell tumours metastasise to para-aortic nodes and to the lungs, giving multiple pulmonary masses.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the chest X-ray findings? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: hard swelling in his right testis
steps.x: A testicular mass and multiple lung lesions in a young man.

elim: Causes nodules and haemoptysis but does not explain the testicular mass.
Unlikely at 22 and does not explain the testis.
Causes hilar lymphadenopathy, not multiple masses with a testicular tumour.
Causes upper-lobe cavitation, usually with fever and weight loss.

steps.x: B. Metastases from a testicular germ cell tumour. Testicular tumour + lung masses = metastases.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with a metastatic non-seminomatous germ cell tumour has severe thoracic back pain for a week. Today his legs feel weak and he has had difficulty passing urine. His temperature is 36.8°C. Power in both legs is 3/5 and there is a sensory level at T10.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe back pain or neurological symptoms in metastatic testicular cancer must raise concern for spinal cord compression, an emergency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Back pain plus cord signs in metastatic disease.

elim: Causes lower motor neurone signs and saddle anaesthesia without a thoracic sensory level.
No sensory level and no back pain from metastases.
Does not cause weakness and a sensory level.
Possible, but known metastases make compression far more likely.

steps.x: D. Metastatic spinal cord compression. Metastatic cancer + back pain + neuro signs = cord compression.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has a hard, painless lump in his left testis for 2 months. His temperature is 36.6°C and there is no lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous solid mass. Radical inguinal orchidectomy is performed. Histology shows a tumour containing embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac and seminoma elements.
questions.q: Which is the most likely classification of this tumour?
questions.e: Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours include yolk sac tumours, embryonal carcinoma, teratoma and mixed germ cell tumours; any non-seminoma element means it is treated as a non-seminoma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely classification of this tumour? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac and seminoma elements
steps.x: Several germ cell components in one tumour.

elim: A stromal tumour, not a germ cell tumour.
Not a germ cell tumour and occurs in older men.
Contains only seminoma and never produces AFP.
A stromal tumour.

steps.x: C. Mixed germ cell tumour. More than one germ cell type = mixed germ cell tumour (a non-seminoma).

questions.stem: A 23 year old footballer was kicked in the scrotum during a match a week ago. The bruising has settled, but while checking himself he found a painless, hard lump in his right testis. His temperature is 36.6°C. The lump does not transilluminate and the epididymis feels normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Trauma often only draws attention to a pre-existing tumour; a painless, hard, non-transilluminating testicular lump in a young man is a germ cell tumour until proven otherwise.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: painless, hard lump in his right testis
steps.x: A painless hard lump found after injury.

elim: Separate from the testis and fluctuant.
Painful with fever and dysuria.
Would be tender and resolving a week after injury, not a painless hard lump.
Sudden severe pain, not a painless lump.

steps.x: C. Testicular germ cell tumour. Injury does not explain a hard painless lump: think tumour.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has noticed a new soft swelling of his right scrotum over 6 weeks. It transilluminates, but the testis inside cannot be palpated clearly. His temperature is 36.7°C. Scrotal ultrasound shows a fluid collection around the testis and a 2 cm solid hypoechoic mass within the testis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: A new hydrocele in a young man can hide an underlying tumour; the solid intratesticular mass on ultrasound is the diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: solid hypoechoic mass within the testis
steps.x: A hydrocele with a solid mass inside the testis.

elim: Lies in the head of the epididymis, separate from the testis.
Painful and febrile.
Extends into the inguinal canal and you cannot get above it.
Does not explain a solid intratesticular mass.

steps.x: E. Testicular tumour. New hydrocele in a young man: scan for an underlying tumour.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has a 4 week history of a painless lump in his left testis. His temperature is 36.6°C. There is a firm nodule in the testis that does not transilluminate. He has been referred urgently and has a scrotal ultrasound.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on scrotal ultrasound?
o: Absent blood flow to the testis
Anechoic cyst in the head of the epididymis
questions.e: First-line scrotal ultrasound shows an intratesticular mass, typically hypoechoic, confirming a solid lesion within the testis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on scrotal ultrasound? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Expect a solid lesion inside the testis.

elim: Describes an epididymal cyst.
Describes a varicocele.
Describes a hydrocele.
Suggests torsion.

steps.x: E. Hypoechoic mass within the testis. Testicular cancer on ultrasound = intratesticular mass.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a solid intratesticular mass on scrotal ultrasound. He is booked for orchidectomy later this week. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 70 bpm. The registrar requests blood tests before surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate set of blood tests to send?
questions.e: Testicular tumour markers are AFP, beta-hCG and LDH (a marker of tumour burden), taken before orchidectomy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate set of blood tests to send? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Germ cell tumour markers.

elim: CA 19-9 and CEA are pancreatic and colorectal markers.
CA-125 is an ovarian marker.
Thyroid and parathyroid markers.
Prostate tests.

steps.x: A. AFP, beta-hCG and LDH. Testicular tumour markers = AFP, hCG, LDH.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has a testicular germ cell tumour. His AFP and beta-hCG are raised. The oncologist wants a marker that gives a measure of the overall bulk of disease rather than the tumour type.
questions.q: Which marker best reflects tumour burden?
questions.e: LDH reflects tumour burden; AFP and beta-hCG help indicate tumour type.

steps.x: The question asks: Which marker best reflects tumour burden? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A non-specific bulk marker.

elim: Reflects bone or liver disease, not germ cell tumour bulk.
Reflects yolk sac elements, a marker of type.
Made by syncytiotrophoblastic cells; it also reflects type.
A colorectal marker.

steps.x: E. Lactate dehydrogenase. LDH = tumour burden.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has a 2.5 cm solid mass within his right testis on ultrasound. His AFP is 120 kU/L (<10). His temperature is 36.6°C. The urologist explains how definitive histology will be obtained.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to obtain a histological diagnosis?
o: Fine needle aspiration of the testis
questions.e: The gold standard is radical inguinal orchidectomy, which gives definitive histology; the testis is never biopsied through the scrotum.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to obtain a histological diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: solid mass within his right testis
steps.x: Histology without breaching the scrotum.

elim: Risks tumour seeding and is not used.
Risks seeding through scrotal skin.
Breaches the scrotum and alters lymphatic drainage.
Risks seeding to the scrotum and inguinal nodes.

steps.x: C. Radical inguinal orchidectomy. Diagnosis and treatment = radical inguinal orchidectomy.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has had a radical inguinal orchidectomy. Histology shows a pure seminoma. His AFP is normal and his beta-hCG is mildly raised. He has no symptoms and his oxygen saturation is 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to stage his disease?
questions.e: Testicular cancer is staged with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, covering para-aortic nodes and lungs.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to stage his disease? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Staging of nodes and lungs.

elim: Misses retroperitoneal nodes.
Bone is not a usual early site.
Not routine staging.
Less sensitive for retroperitoneal nodes and does not image the chest.

steps.x: B. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis. Staging = CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has a slowly growing, smooth, firm mass in his right testis. Ultrasound shows a homogeneous intratesticular mass. He is told the tumour is likely to be a pure seminoma. His temperature is 36.5°C.
questions.q: Which tumour marker result is most likely?
o: Markedly raised AFP with normal beta-hCG
Normal AFP with a normal or mildly raised beta-hCG
questions.e: Pure seminoma never makes AFP; beta-hCG may be raised because some seminomas contain syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells.

steps.x: The question asks: Which tumour marker result is most likely? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A pure seminoma's marker profile.

elim: A raised AFP indicates yolk sac elements, never pure seminoma.
An ovarian marker.
A prostate marker.
AFP is never produced by pure seminoma.

steps.x: D. Normal AFP with a normal or mildly raised beta-hCG. Pure seminoma: AFP normal, hCG may be raised.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man is on surveillance after orchidectomy for a stage I non-seminoma. He feels well. His AFP has risen on two consecutive tests to 48 kU/L (<10), having been normal for a year. His temperature is 36.7°C and examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: No investigation, repeat marker in 1 year
Repeat scrotal ultrasound of the remaining testis only
questions.e: Surveillance uses tumour markers and imaging; a rising AFP suggests relapse and is restaged with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A rising marker on surveillance.

elim: A rising AFP on surveillance signals relapse.
Not the first site to image.
Does not look for metastatic relapse.
Not needed; image for relapse.

steps.x: A. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis. Rising markers = restage with CT CAP.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man completed BEP chemotherapy for a metastatic non-seminoma 8 months ago. He now has 2 weeks of severe lumbar back pain that wakes him at night and, since this morning, numbness in both legs. His temperature is 36.7°C. Leg reflexes are brisk and there is reduced sensation below L1.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: CT of the abdomen in 4 weeks
Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
Urgent MRI of the whole spine
questions.e: Severe back pain or neurological symptoms in metastatic testicular cancer raise concern for spinal cord compression, investigated with urgent whole-spine MRI.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Back pain plus new neurology in a man with metastatic cancer.

elim: Too slow for suspected cord compression.
Not used and potentially harmful with a compressive lesion.
For peripheral neuropathy, not cord compression.
Insensitive and does not show the cord.

steps.x: E. Urgent MRI of the whole spine. Suspected cord compression = urgent whole-spine MRI.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man sees his GP with a painless lump in his right testis noticed 2 weeks ago. His temperature is 36.6°C. There is a hard nodule within the testis that does not transilluminate. He has no urinary symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: NICE NG12: any suspicious testicular mass is referred urgently via the 2-week-wait pathway.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A suspicious mass in primary care.

elim: There is no evidence of infection; this delays a cancer referral.
A suspicious mass needs urgent referral.
Too slow for a suspicious mass.
Never biopsy through the scrotum.

steps.x: E. Urgent 2-week-wait urology referral. Suspicious testicular mass = 2WW referral.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a hard right testicular mass. Ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular lesion and his beta-hCG is raised. CT shows no spread. He asks what operation is planned and how it will be done.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Partial orchidectomy through a scrotal incision
questions.e: First-line management is radical inguinal orchidectomy, removing the testis and cord through the groin.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Localised disease needing definitive surgery.

elim: Breaches the scrotum.
Histology and removal come first.
Considered later for residual nodal disease.
Breaches the scrotum, altering lymphatic drainage.

steps.x: B. Radical inguinal orchidectomy. First-line = radical inguinal orchidectomy.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has had a radical inguinal orchidectomy for a pure seminoma. His AFP is normal. CT shows a single 1.5 cm para-aortic lymph node and no other disease. He is fit and well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: Seminoma is highly radiosensitive, so after orchidectomy it is treated with radiotherapy or chemotherapy such as carboplatin.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next treatment? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Small-volume nodal seminoma.

elim: An anti-androgen for prostate cancer.
A GnRH agonist for prostate cancer.
He has nodal disease that needs treatment.
Used for residual non-seminoma, not radiosensitive seminoma.

steps.x: D. Radiotherapy to the para-aortic nodes. Seminoma after orchidectomy: radiotherapy or carboplatin.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man is starting chemotherapy after orchidectomy for a metastatic teratoma. He is a keen runner. The oncologist arranges baseline lung function tests because one drug in his regimen can cause pulmonary fibrosis.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Non-seminomas are treated with BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin); bleomycin can cause pulmonary fibrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which drug is most likely responsible? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
The 'B' in BEP.

elim: Used for seminoma; mainly causes myelosuppression.
Causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
Mainly causes myelosuppression.
Not used for testicular cancer.

steps.x: A. Bleomycin. BEP: bleomycin lung toxicity.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has had an orchidectomy for a mixed germ cell tumour. CT shows enlarged para-aortic nodes and several lung nodules. His AFP is 1200 kU/L (<10) and beta-hCG is 900 IU/L (<5). His oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: Non-seminomatous germ cell tumours are treated with combination chemotherapy, BEP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next treatment? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Metastatic non-seminoma.

elim: Used for seminoma, not metastatic non-seminoma.
Used for low-volume seminoma, not metastatic non-seminoma.
He has metastatic disease.
Not a testicular cancer treatment.

steps.x: A. BEP chemotherapy. Non-seminoma = BEP.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man with a newly diagnosed testicular germ cell tumour is booked for radical inguinal orchidectomy and will probably need chemotherapy afterwards. He and his partner hope to have children in the future.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate step before treatment?
questions.e: Infertility is a complication of testicular cancer and its treatment, so sperm banking is offered before orchidectomy and chemotherapy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate step before treatment? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Protect future fertility.

elim: Delaying cancer surgery is unsafe.
Suppresses spermatogenesis and is not indicated.
Unnecessary and removes all fertility.
Infertility is a recognised complication.

steps.x: B. Offer sperm banking. Before treatment: sperm banking.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man noticed a painless, hard lump in his right testis 6 weeks ago. Ultrasound showed a solid intratesticular mass and he has a radical orchidectomy. The pathologist reports a germ cell tumour and explains that it has arisen from the cells that normally produce sperm.
questions.q: From which tissue did this tumour most likely arise?
o: Germinal epithelium of the seminiferous tubules
questions.e: Germ cell tumours arise from malignant transformation of the germinal epithelium of the seminiferous tubules.

steps.x: The question asks: From which tissue did this tumour most likely arise? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
The sperm-producing cells.

elim: Not the source of germ cell tumours.
Give rise to stromal tumours.
Give rise to Sertoli cell tumours.
Lines the scrotal sac; it forms hydroceles and mesotheliomas.

steps.x: B. Germinal epithelium of the seminiferous tubules. Germ cell tumours come from the seminiferous tubule germinal epithelium.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man had an orchidopexy at age 4 for a left undescended testis. He asks whether the operation means his cancer risk is now the same as other men's. Both testes are normal on examination today.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate statement about his risk?
o: His risk is lower than average
His risk is normal after orchidopexy
His risk remains raised despite the orchidopexy
Only the right testis is at increased risk
Risk is raised only before puberty
questions.e: Higher intra-abdominal temperature impairs germ cell maturation, which predisposes to malignant transformation even after orchidopexy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most accurate statement about his risk? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Previous cryptorchidism treated surgically.

elim: Cryptorchidism raises risk.
Orchidopexy does not remove the risk.
The undescended testis carries the greatest risk.
Testicular cancer peaks at 15 to 35.

steps.x: C. His risk remains raised despite the orchidopexy. Cryptorchidism risk persists after orchidopexy.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has a stage II seminoma with two enlarged para-aortic nodes on CT. His AFP is normal. After orchidectomy he has radiotherapy to the para-aortic nodes, and the nodes disappear completely. He asks why his tumour responded so well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Slow growth making cells resistant to radiation
Uniform cells resembling primordial germ cells that are highly radiosensitive
questions.e: Seminoma is made of relatively uniform cells resembling primordial germ cells, which are highly radiosensitive; this is part of why it has a better prognosis than teratoma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Why seminoma melts with radiotherapy.

elim: Describes non-seminomas, which are less radiosensitive.
Seminomas do not produce AFP.
Seminoma is not treated with hormones.
Slow growth does not explain radiosensitivity.

steps.x: E. Uniform cells resembling primordial germ cells that are highly radiosensitive. Seminoma = uniform, primordial-germ-cell-like and radiosensitive.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man has a teratoma with para-aortic and lung metastases at diagnosis, 6 weeks after he first noticed the lump. His brother's friend had a seminoma that stayed in the testis for a year. He asks why his tumour behaved so differently.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Non-seminomas are made of uniform primordial germ cells
Non-seminomas contain heterogeneous, less differentiated tissue
Teratomas only occur in undescended testes
questions.e: Non-seminomatous tumours contain heterogeneous, less differentiated elements (yolk sac, embryonal, choriocarcinoma, teratoma), so they grow and spread faster.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: stayed in the testis for a year
steps.x: Fast versus slow behaviour.

elim: Describes seminoma.
They are germ cell tumours.
Seminoma is the radiosensitive tumour.
Cryptorchidism raises risk but is not required.

steps.x: D. Non-seminomas contain heterogeneous, less differentiated tissue. Non-seminomas are heterogeneous and less differentiated, so more aggressive.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has an orchidectomy. The first histology report suggests a pure seminoma, but his AFP before surgery was 260 kU/L (<10) (see item resources). The oncologist asks for the specimen to be re-examined.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the raised AFP?
o: Unrecognised yolk sac elements in the tumour
questions.e: AFP is made by yolk sac elements and never by pure seminoma, so a raised AFP means non-seminomatous elements are present.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for the raised AFP? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A raised AFP that does not fit the histology.

elim: Does not produce AFP.
Pure seminoma never produces AFP.
His AFP was taken before surgery.
These produce beta-hCG, not AFP.

steps.x: E. Unrecognised yolk sac elements in the tumour. Raised AFP = yolk sac elements, never pure seminoma.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man with a seminoma diagnosed after orchidectomy has had 2 months of tender breast enlargement. His beta-hCG is 140 IU/L (<5) and AFP is normal. Histology shows scattered large multinucleated cells among the seminoma cells.
questions.q: Which cells are most likely producing the beta-hCG?
questions.e: Beta-hCG is produced by syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells, present in some seminomas and in choriocarcinoma; hCG raises the oestrogen:androgen ratio, causing gynaecomastia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which cells are most likely producing the beta-hCG? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
hCG and giant cells in a seminoma.

elim: Make testosterone, not hCG.
Support spermatogenesis and make inhibin.
Do not produce hCG.
Produce AFP, not hCG.

steps.x: D. Syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells. hCG = syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man has a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour and has noticed swelling of both breasts. He takes no medicines and does not use cannabis or anabolic steroids. His beta-hCG is markedly raised. His liver function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his breast enlargement?
questions.e: Gynaecomastia in testicular cancer reflects an increased oestrogen:androgen ratio, driven by hCG.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his breast enlargement? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Breast growth with a hormone-secreting tumour.

elim: Not the mechanism here.
His liver function is normal.
Would not cause gynaecomastia.
Excess testosterone alone does not explain it.

steps.x: B. Increased oestrogen to androgen ratio. Gynaecomastia = raised oestrogen:androgen ratio.
